title: How Corsets Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore the history and mechanics of corsets, from ancient Crete and medieval stays through the 18th and 19th centuries, the Gibson Girl and swan bill corset, the Warner Brothers' health corset, and the decline after World War One. They explain corset construction (busk, boning channels, cutil fabric, lacing styles including bidirectional and ladder lacing, and bunny ears), discuss waist training and extreme tight lacing, and bust myths such as rib removal and fainting. They discuss Cathy Young, a record holder for smallest living waist, and the male-dominated and gender questions around corseting. The episode closes with a listener mail about pain scales in veterinary medicine.

segments.title: Opening banter and feelings about extreme corseting
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with nervousness and mixed feelings about corsets and extreme tight lacing, including Cathy Young and whether the practice is a sexist pressure or an individual choice.

segments.title: Waist training and safety
segments.summary: The hosts define waist training as reshaping the body over about a decade rather than losing weight, note that corsets should not hurt, and mention Cathy Young's advice to go slowly.

segments.title: Ancient and medieval origins of the corset
segments.summary: The hosts trace early body-shaping garments from ancient Crete, the medieval heavy stay, and the shift from tubular to conical corset shapes in the eighteenth century.

segments.title: Corsets in fashion, Warner Brothers and whalebone to steel
segments.summary: Corsets were mainstream fashion until World War One. The Warner Brothers, anti-corset doctors from Bridgeport, Connecticut, made a health corset, and the hosts discuss the Von Sömmerring article behind corset myths and the switch from whalebone to steel.

segments.title: Gibson Girl and the swan bill corset
segments.summary: Charles Dana Gibson popularized the Gibson Girl in the 1890s, drawn in swan bill corsets derived from a corset by Dr. Ines Ghosh. The hosts describe its posture problems and the trend's brief run before World War One and the flapper era.

segments.title: Corset revival and designers
segments.summary: After the flapper era, corsets faded, with a brief Christian Dior revival in the 1940s. Vivienne Westwood and Jean Paul Gaultier later brought corsets back as outerwear, with Madonna cited as a promoter.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short break before the discussion continues.

segments.title: Corset construction: busk, boning, cutil, and lacing
segments.summary: The hosts describe corset parts: cutil cotton fabric, boning channels, the busk at the front, the stomacher, and lacing methods including bidirectional lacing, ladder lacing, and bunny ears for self-lacing. They also discuss fit and sizing advice from Orchard Corsets.

segments.title: Cathy Young, Ethel Granger, and corset myths
segments.summary: Cathy Young is a Guinness record holder for the smallest living waist at 15 inches, and she began waist training at 48. Ethel Granger's 13-inch waist is cited as the narrowest on record. The hosts discuss a creepy husband in Cathy Young's FAQ, the myth of surgical rib removal, and the Victorian fainting myth.

segments.title: Corsets, men, and the sign-off on girdles
segments.summary: The hosts discuss men wearing corsets, which was viewed with suspicion in the nineteenth century, the idea of patriarchal pressure, and the later replacement of corsets by girdles and men's shapewear.

segments.title: Listener mail: pain scales in animals
segments.summary: A listener writes about pain scales in veterinary medicine, how dogs and cats hide pain, and the historical belief that animals did not feel pain.

segments.title: Outro and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, mention possible live shows, and give social media and email contact details.
